祖烈者可得而敷張其盛矣粵自三五而上聖
神代作道化渾淪君臣之告誡皆心學之
精朝堂之須布即大道之要故堯之告舜
曰允執厥中舜之告禹曰人心惟危道心
惟微惟精惟一允執厥中堯舜之所以事
其心者如是而已務學之名未前聞也當
時史臣之贊曰元首明哉股肱良哉庶事
punctuated:
民之衆，咸求治於人君之一身，使非政以運之，何以兼統而無外？天下之政亦大矣，萬幾之裁，庶務之理，咸取足於人君之一心，使非學以主之，何以會應而不窮？故齊衆軌物，政之會經也，非學無以裕其基；崇志廣業，學之懿則也，非政無以達其用。是二者固相須也，而皆管攝于一心。心也者，又政之樞紐而學之本原也。知乎此，可以論古帝王之政之學，而我二祖之所以匹休帝王，與皇上之作求世德，以光揚于祖烈者，可得而敷張其盛矣。
粵自三五而上，聖神代作，道化渾淪，君臣之告誡皆心學之精，朝堂之須布即大道之要。故堯之告舜曰：「允執厥中。」舜之告禹曰：「人心惟危，道心惟微，惟精惟一，允執厥中。」堯舜之所以事其心者，如是而已，務學之名未前聞也。當時史臣之贊曰：「元首明哉，股肱良哉，庶事
translation_en:
…the multitude of the people all look for good government to the single person of the ruler. Unless he employs governance to manage them, how can he bring them all under his rule, leaving none outside? The affairs of government throughout the realm are likewise vast. Decisions on the myriad affairs and the ordering of all business depend entirely upon the ruler’s single mind. Unless learning guides it, how can he respond to everything without exhaustion? Thus, bringing the multitude into order and setting standards for all things are the comprehensive principles of governance; without learning, its foundations cannot be enriched. Elevating one’s aspirations and extending one’s accomplishments are the excellent standards of learning; without governance, its practical benefits cannot be realized. These two assuredly depend upon each other, and both are governed by the single mind. The mind, moreover, is the pivot of governance and the source of learning. Understanding this, we may discuss the governance and learning of the ancient emperors and kings, and fully expound the greatness of how our two ancestral emperors equaled them in glory, and how His Majesty seeks out the virtue transmitted through the generations to illuminate his ancestors’ glorious achievements.
From the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors back into earlier antiquity, sages of divine understanding arose in succession, and transformation through the Way formed an undivided whole. The admonitions exchanged between rulers and ministers were all the essence of learning concerning the mind; what was promulgated at court [?] was itself the essential substance of the Great Way. Thus Yao told Shun: “Truly hold fast to the Mean.” Shun told Yu: “The human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle. Be discerning, be single-minded; truly hold fast to the Mean.” This was all that Yao and Shun did to cultivate their minds; the designation ‘devotion to learning’ had not yet been heard. The court historians of that time offered this praise: “How enlightened is the head! How worthy are the limbs! The manifold affairs…”

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
康哉孔子亦曰無爲而治恭已正南面而
已勤政之名未前聞也至皐陶之戒禹曰
兢兢業業一日二日萬幾後之言勤政者
昉焉然其克勤克儉之政即惟幾惟康之
學是純王之政也若湯之昧爽丕顯文之
不遑暇食非與禹一揆者耶傅說之告高
宗曰學于古訓乃有獲後之言務學者昉
焉然以恭默思道之學爲不僭不濫之政
是純王之學也若中宗之嚴恭寅畏成王
===
之緝熙光明非與高宗一揆者耶秦不師
古先王之政之學蕩然滅矣漢興以來有
志於治者非不勵精政務然漢宣帝齋居
決事而所尚者刑名唐太宗日昃罷朝而
所慚者内德宋眞宗詢問政事夜以繼日
而封禪禱祀不免侈心是政焉而不本於
學非帝王之所謂政也亦有志於學者非
不崇尚儒術然明帝几杖執業而所師者
桓榮玄宗更日侍讀而所親者馬褚哲宗
punctuated:
康哉！」孔子亦曰：「無爲而治，恭已正南面而已。」勤政之名未前聞也。至皐陶之戒禹曰：「兢兢業業，一日二日萬幾。」後之言勤政者昉焉。然其克勤克儉之政，即惟幾惟康之學，是純王之政也。若湯之昧爽丕顯，文之不遑暇食，非與禹一揆者耶？傅說之告高宗曰：「學于古訓，乃有獲。」後之言務學者昉焉。然以恭默思道之學，爲不僭不濫之政，是純王之學也。若中宗之嚴恭寅畏，成王之緝熙光明，非與高宗一揆者耶？

秦不師古，先王之政之學蕩然滅矣。漢興以來，有志於治者非不勵精政務，然漢宣帝齋居決事，而所尚者刑名；唐太宗日昃罷朝，而所慚者内德；宋眞宗詢問政事，夜以繼日，而封禪禱祀，不免侈心。是政焉而不本於學，非帝王之所謂政也。亦有志於學者，非不崇尚儒術，然明帝几杖執業，而所師者桓榮；玄宗更日侍讀，而所親者馬褚；哲宗
translation_en:
…prosperous indeed!” Confucius likewise said: “He governed without action, merely holding himself reverently and facing due south.” The expression “diligence in government” had not previously been heard. It was when Gao Yao admonished Yu, saying, “Be watchful and diligent: in a single day or two there are myriad incipient matters to attend to,” that later discussions of diligence in government found their origin. Yet Yu’s government, marked by diligence and frugality, was itself the learning that attends to incipient developments and seeks well-being. This was the government of a true sage king. Were Tang’s conspicuous virtue from daybreak and King Wen’s having no leisure even to eat not guided by the same principle as Yu’s? Fu Yue told Gaozong: “Study the teachings of antiquity, and then you will gain understanding.” Here later discussions of devotion to learning found their origin. Yet Gaozong made his learning—reverent silence and contemplation of the Way—the basis of government in which rewards were not misplaced and punishments were not excessive. This was the learning of a true sage king. Were Zhongzong’s solemn reverence and vigilant awe, and King Cheng’s sustained and radiant brightness, not guided by the same principle as Gaozong’s?

Qin did not take antiquity as its teacher, and the government and learning of the former kings were utterly swept away. Since the rise of Han, rulers intent on good government have certainly applied themselves energetically to administrative affairs. Yet although Emperor Xuandi of Han withdrew in solemn seclusion to decide affairs, what he prized was penal and administrative technique. Although Taizong of Tang held court until the sun was declining, his inner virtue gave him cause for shame. Although Zhenzong of Song inquired into affairs of government by night as well as by day, his sacrifices to Heaven and Earth at Mount Tai and his prayers and offerings betrayed an extravagant disposition. This was government without a foundation in learning; it was not what the sage emperors and kings meant by government. There were also rulers intent on learning, who certainly esteemed Confucian teachings. Yet although Emperor Mingdi honored his teacher with an armrest and staff and received instruction, the man he took as his teacher was Huan Rong. Although Xuanzong had readers-in-waiting attend him on alternate days, those he held close were Ma and Chu. Zhezong…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
首召大儒說書崇政而正心誠意不免歟
聞是學焉而無裨於政非帝王之所謂學
也洪惟我
太祖高皇帝開天創業邁三五之治功
成祖文皇帝靖內定基奠萬年之洪業其憂勤
庶政闡揚至理而敷諸
聖訓諭答諸臣直與典謨相表裏者
太祖嘗謂學士宋濂曰朕之爲君上畏天地下
畏兆民兢兢業業不敢自逸又謂侍臣曰人
君日理萬幾怠心一生則庶務壅滯其貽患
===
不可勝言而又置尚書洪範於座右而親爲
註釋揭大學衍義於兩廡而時令講析此
其勤政務學之心何如也
成祖嘗答侍臣曰朕在禁中周思庶事或一事
未行或行之未善即不寐至旦嘗謂學士解
縉曰朕退朝默坐未嘗不思管束此心但於
宮室車馬服食玩好無所增加則天下自然
無事矣而又作
punctuated:
首召大儒說書崇政，而正心誠意不免歟聞。是學焉而無裨於政，非帝王之所謂學也。
洪惟我太祖高皇帝開天創業，邁三五之治功；成祖文皇帝靖內定基，奠萬年之洪業。其憂勤庶政，闡揚至理，而敷諸聖訓，諭答諸臣，直與典謨相表裏者。
太祖嘗謂學士宋濂曰：「朕之爲君，上畏天地，下畏兆民，兢兢業業，不敢自逸。」又謂侍臣曰：「人君日理萬幾，怠心一生，則庶務壅滯，其貽患不可勝言。」而又置尚書洪範於座右，而親爲註釋；揭大學衍義於兩廡，而時令講析。此其勤政務學之心何如也！
成祖嘗答侍臣曰：「朕在禁中，周思庶事，或一事未行，或行之未善，即不寐至旦。」嘗謂學士解縉曰：「朕退朝默坐，未嘗不思管束此心。但於宮室、車馬、服食、玩好無所增加，則天下自然無事矣。」而又作
translation_en:
…first summoned eminent Confucian scholars to expound the books in Chongzheng Hall, yet could not help finding talk of rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere unwelcome [?]. Such learning brought no benefit to government; it was not what true emperors and kings understood by learning.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao inaugurated a new order and founded the dynasty, surpassing the achievements in government of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors. Emperor Chengzu Wen pacified the realm and secured its foundations, establishing a grand enterprise to endure for ten thousand years. Their anxious diligence in all affairs of government and their elucidation of the highest principles, expressed in their sacred instructions and in their pronouncements and replies to their ministers, directly complement the Canons and Counsels of the Book of Documents.
Taizu once told Academician Song Lian: “As ruler, above I stand in awe of Heaven and Earth; below I stand in awe of the myriad people. Ever vigilant and conscientious, I dare not indulge in ease.” He also told his attendant ministers: “A ruler attends each day to countless affairs. Once an idle thought arises, all business becomes obstructed, and the resulting harm is beyond telling.” Moreover, he placed the “Great Plan” chapter of the Book of Documents beside his seat and personally annotated it. He displayed the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning in the two side galleries and periodically ordered it to be expounded and analyzed. How devoted was his heart to diligent government and earnest learning!
Chengzu once replied to his attendant ministers: “Within the palace, I ponder all affairs thoroughly. If even one matter has not been carried out, or has been carried out poorly, I cannot sleep until dawn.” He once told Academician Xie Jin: “When I withdraw from court and sit in silence, I invariably consider how to keep this mind under control. If only there is no increase in palaces, carriages and horses, clothing and food, or objects of pleasure, then all under Heaven will naturally be at peace.” He also composed…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖學心法以會百王之要纂經書性理以𢑱
諸儒之大全此其勤政務學之心何如也
列聖相承以及
世宗肅皇帝政秉勵精學傳敬一享祚長久致
治昇平乃篤啓我
皇上以
神聖之資紹帝王之統自
登極之初首發
德音與民更始
===
聖政之寛仁固天下所共戴者而又節用愛人
儉符夏禹遇災
省己誠切殷湯
臨朝遵昧爽之規
納諫存包荒之量一念勤政之心揆之
二祖豈異耶自
藩邸之年日親儒彥論道陳經
聖學之資深固天下所共仰者而又
詔開經筵數陳治理
punctuated: 《聖學心法》，以會百王之要；纂經書性理，以𢑱諸儒之大全。此其勤政務學之心何如也？列聖相承，以及世宗肅皇帝，政秉勵精，學傳敬一，享祚長久，致治昇平，乃篤啓我皇上，以神聖之資，紹帝王之統。自登極之初，首發德音，與民更始。聖政之寛仁，固天下所共戴者，而又節用愛人，儉符夏禹；遇災省己，誠切殷湯；臨朝遵昧爽之規，納諫存包荒之量。一念勤政之心，揆之二祖，豈異耶？自藩邸之年，日親儒彥，論道陳經。聖學之資深，固天下所共仰者，而又詔開經筵，數陳治理，
translation_en:
…The Mind-Method of Sagely Learning (Shengxue xinfa), to bring together the essentials of the hundred kings; he also compiled the classics and writings on human nature and principle, to assemble [?] the comprehensive learning of the Confucian scholars. How great was his devotion to diligent government and earnest study!

The successive sage emperors carried on this legacy down to Shizong, the Solemn Emperor. In government he upheld vigorous application; in learning he transmitted reverent single-mindedness. He enjoyed a long reign and brought about peaceful and flourishing rule, thereby laying a firm foundation for our present Emperor, who, endowed with sagely and divine gifts, succeeded to the imperial line. At the very beginning of his accession, he first issued a gracious proclamation to make a fresh start together with the people. The magnanimity and benevolence of his sagely government are indeed acclaimed by all under Heaven. Moreover, he restrains expenditure and cherishes the people, matching Yu of the Xia in frugality; when disasters occur, he examines himself, with sincerity as earnest as Tang of the Shang. He observes the rule of holding court before dawn and receives remonstrance with the magnanimity to embrace even the uncultivated. Measured against the two founding ancestors, how does his single-minded devotion to diligent government differ?

From his years in the princely residence, he daily associated with eminent Confucian scholars, discussing the Way and expounding the classics. The depth of his attainment in sagely learning is indeed admired by all under Heaven. Moreover, he has ordered the Classics Colloquium to convene, with frequent presentations on the principles of government…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
躬勤日講啓沃乃心
視學隆師儒之禮
賜賚及聖賢之裔上念務學之心揆之
二祖豈異耶夫務學則道揆明于上勤政則膏
澤下于民天下之人延頸跂踵思見德化
之成此誠
宗社無疆之慶太平有象之徵矣然勤始而
慮終者明君之盛節弭憂治而危明者藎
臣之良圖也故益之戒舜曰罔失法度罔
===
遊于逸罔淫于樂皐陶之戒禹曰無教逸
欲有邦夫舜禹大聖豈有遊樂之事逸欲
之教乎而二臣言之者誠以有一於此荒
政廢學之端也故戒之不可不預耳他若
漢之文帝賢君也敦朴勤儉一無嗜慾偶
好射獵而賈誼切諫誼書帝之備者誠愛
帝之全也
皇上今之舜禹無論漢文而執事進策諸生猶
咨以論思之助是即伯益皐陶之心也愚
banxin: 鄉試錄　一　李八
punctuated:
躬勤日講，啓沃乃心；視學隆師儒之禮，賜賚及聖賢之裔。上念務學之心，揆之二祖，豈異耶？夫務學則道揆明于上，勤政則膏澤下于民。天下之人延頸跂踵，思見德化之成，此誠宗社無疆之慶、太平有象之徵矣。然勤始而慮終者，明君之盛節；弭憂治而危明者，藎臣之良圖也。故益之戒舜曰：「罔失法度，罔遊于逸，罔淫于樂。」皐陶之戒禹曰：「無教逸欲有邦。」夫舜禹大聖，豈有遊樂之事、逸欲之教乎？而二臣言之者，誠以有一於此，荒政廢學之端也，故戒之不可不預耳。他若漢之文帝，賢君也，敦朴勤儉，一無嗜慾，偶好射獵，而賈誼切諫。誼書帝之備者，誠愛帝之全也。
皇上今之舜禹，無論漢文，而執事進策諸生，猶咨以論思之助，是即伯益皐陶之心也。愚
translation_en:
…He diligently attends the daily lectures in person, allowing instruction to nourish his mind. In visiting the academy, he honors teachers and scholars with heightened ceremony; his gifts extend to the descendants of sages and worthies. How does His Majesty’s commitment to learning differ from that of the two ancestral emperors? Through devotion to learning, the principles governing the Way become clear above; through diligence in government, beneficence flows down to the people. All under Heaven crane their necks and stand on tiptoe, longing to witness the fulfillment of his moral transformation. This is truly a boundless blessing for the dynastic altars and a visible portent of great peace. Yet to begin diligently and consider the outcome is the noble conduct of an enlightened ruler; to avert anxieties amid good order and remain alert to danger [?] is the sound counsel of a devoted minister. Thus Yi admonished Shun: “Do not depart from the laws and standards; do not wander into idleness; do not indulge excessively in pleasure.” Gao Yao admonished Yu: “Do not teach those who hold domains to pursue ease and desire.” Now Shun and Yu were great sages: could they possibly have pursued amusement or taught indulgence in ease and desire? These two ministers nevertheless spoke because even one such failing would mark the beginning of neglecting government and abandoning learning. Hence admonition must be given beforehand.
Consider also Emperor Wen of the Han, a worthy ruler. He was earnest, unassuming, diligent, and frugal, without any consuming appetites. Yet when he occasionally took pleasure in hunting, Jia Yi remonstrated earnestly. Jia Yi’s writing concerning the emperor’s completeness [?] arose from his sincere wish to preserve the emperor’s perfection.
His Majesty is the Shun or Yu of our age, surpassing any comparison with Emperor Wen of the Han. Yet you gentlemen, in putting policy questions to the students, still seek the assistance of their deliberations. This is precisely the spirit of Bo Yi and Gao Yao. I, in my humble…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
主賤且遠敢附於賈生之義僭陳其愚焉
謂政事以賞不以文學問貴恒不貴暫夫
堂陛森嚴而上下之情不交百司庶府代天
工而分理者容有奏牘所不能悉而請對
無階者乎
宸旒咫尺而咨訪之音不格左右侍從陳經
史而勸講者容有獻納所不能盡而待問
未已者乎封事可否悉付中書天下仰
朝廷之公矣然必參之以獨斷所以收明作
===
之功諸司建白並荷含容天下仰
朝廷之明矣然必繼之以允蹈所以彰納諫
之實程伯淳謂大臣之職惟在輔養君德
今也召見無閒論道奚自將何以為輔養
之資然則
祖宗顧問之舊所當復乎司馬光謂人君之職
不當詳覽細務今也章疏塡委省覽為勞
將何以為易簡之要然則宋臣貼黃之規
所可循乎學無顯隱宥密之地必有以為
punctuated: 主賤且遠，敢附於賈生之義，僭陳其愚焉。謂政事以賞不以文，學問貴恒不貴暫。夫堂陛森嚴，而上下之情不交；百司庶府代天工而分理者，容有奏牘所不能悉，而請對無階者乎？宸旒咫尺，而咨訪之音不格；左右侍從陳經史而勸講者，容有獻納所不能盡，而待問未已者乎？封事可否，悉付中書，天下仰朝廷之公矣；然必參之以獨斷，所以收明作之功。諸司建白，並荷含容，天下仰朝廷之明矣；然必繼之以允蹈，所以彰納諫之實。程伯淳謂大臣之職，惟在輔養君德。今也召見無閒，論道奚自？將何以為輔養之資？然則祖宗顧問之舊，所當復乎？司馬光謂人君之職，不當詳覽細務。今也章疏塡委，省覽為勞，將何以為易簡之要？然則宋臣貼黃之規，所可循乎？學無顯隱，宥密之地，必有以為
translation_en:
…lowly and far removed [the opening character is doubtful], I venture to follow the spirit of Master Jia and presumptuously set forth my humble views. I maintain that government should proceed through rewards [?], rather than mere formalities, and that learning requires constancy rather than intermittent effort. The hall and steps of the throne inspire solemn awe, yet the feelings of ruler and subjects do not pass between them. Among the officials of the many offices who perform Heaven’s work and share responsibility for administration, might there be some whose written submissions cannot convey everything, yet who have no means of requesting an audience? The imperial presence is but inches away, yet no words of inquiry reach them. Among the attendants who expound the classics and histories and lecture to the ruler, might there be some whose counsel cannot be fully expressed, and who still await his questions?

Decisions on sealed memorials are all entrusted to the Secretariat, and all under Heaven look up to the court’s impartiality. Yet the ruler must supplement this with his own judgment, so as to achieve the results of enlightened action. The proposals of the various offices all receive a tolerant hearing, and all under Heaven look up to the court’s discernment. Yet genuine implementation must follow, so as to manifest the reality of accepting remonstrance. Cheng Bochun said that the duty of great ministers lies solely in assisting and nurturing the ruler’s virtue. If there is now no opportunity for summoned audiences, how can discussion of the Way take place? What means will there be to assist and nurture his virtue? Should not, then, the ancestral practice of consulting ministers be restored?

Sima Guang said that a ruler’s duties should not include examining minor affairs in detail. Now memorials pile up, and their examination is a burden: how can the essentials of ease and simplicity in government be attained? Might the practice of attaching yellow-paper summaries, used by Song ministers, therefore be followed? Learning makes no distinction between public and private settings; in the secluded depths of the palace, there must be a means to serve as…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
基命之本者故出入起居罔有不𢿅所以
謹獨也道有張弛清燕之暇必有以爲適
情之資者故左右暬御罔非正人所以慎
動也是數者所謂政之樞紐學之本原而
皆求諸心者也程子曰聖學以正心爲要
孟子曰唯大人爲能格君心之非是在
聖君賢相相與以有成者草茅賤士何幸躬逢
其盛
第二問
===
胡文衢
同考試官知縣王　批〔論書二法聖人作之以風世子能綜核始末評品〕〔心跡深知周孔立法之原且歸之恭眾論𥨊往牒燬鑒可行非徒〕
空言無當者佳士佳士
考試官左中允孫　批〔聖人以公心垂遠慮無踰論書二者子能深究法原在欲使人有所畏而〕〔不爲不善誠教善之微權也是可錄矣〕
考試官左諭德王　批〔發明二聖教天下之心精〕
punctuated:
基命之本者，故出入起居罔有不𢿅，所以謹獨也。道有張弛，清燕之暇必有以爲適情之資者，故左右暬御罔非正人，所以慎動也。是數者，所謂政之樞紐、學之本原，而皆求諸心者也。程子曰：「聖學以正心爲要。」孟子曰：「唯大人爲能格君心之非。」是在聖君賢相相與以有成者，草茅賤士何幸躬逢其盛！
第二問
胡文衢
同考試官知縣王，批〔論書二法，聖人作之以風世。子能綜核始末，評品〕〔心跡，深知周孔立法之原，且歸之恭眾論、𥨊往牒、燬鑒可行，非徒〕空言無當者。佳士！佳士！
考試官左中允孫，批〔聖人以公心垂遠慮，無踰論書二者。子能深究法原，在欲使人有所畏而〕〔不爲不善，誠教善之微權也。是可錄矣。〕
考試官左諭德王，批〔發明二聖教天下之心，精〕
translation_en:
…the foundation for establishing the Mandate. Thus, in going out and coming in, in rising and resting, there is nothing lacking in reverence [?]: this is how one exercises vigilance when alone. The Way has its times of tension and relaxation; in the leisure of quiet retirement, there must be means of giving fitting scope to the feelings. Thus all attendants serving at one's side must be upright people: this is how one exercises care in one's actions. These several matters are what are called the pivots of government and the roots of learning, and all are to be sought within the heart. Master Cheng said, “The essential point of the learning of the sages is to rectify the heart.” Mencius said, “Only a great man can correct what is wrong in the ruler's heart.” Accomplishing this rests with a sage ruler and worthy ministers working together. How fortunate is a humble scholar from the countryside to witness such flourishing in person!
Second Policy Question
Hu Wenqu (胡文衢)
Associate Examiner Wang, District Magistrate, comments: “The two methods of discourse [?] and historical writing were established by the sages to influence the world. You can comprehensively examine their beginnings and ends and assess intentions and actions, deeply understanding the original purposes for which the Duke of Zhou and Confucius established these methods. Moreover, you bring these back to respecting public opinion [?], setting aside earlier records [?], and destroying mirrors [?] as practicable measures, rather than merely offering empty words without application. A worthy scholar! A worthy scholar!”
Examiner Sun, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: “For the sages' impartial concern extending into the distant future, nothing surpasses these two things, discourse [?] and historical writing. You can investigate deeply the original purpose of these methods: to give people something to fear so that they refrain from wrongdoing. This is indeed a subtle expedient for teaching goodness. This deserves selection.”
Examiner Wang, Left Admonisher, comments: “You elucidate the intentions of the two sages in teaching the world, with precision…”

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
詳懇到而詞復高古殆非凡士
聖人敎天下之心甚無已也故有謚法以
定當人之稱名而榮辱判有書法以紀當
世之事實而勸戒昭聖人何心哉聖人敎
天下以善而天下率焉至願也顧乃有不
盡然者於是不得已而有慶與刑然慶與
刑或有所不及況行之一時未能明白㬎
著於萬世也於是不得已而有謚與書故
謚以定稱名別榮辱非為一世設也而考
之書益詳書以紀事實垂勸戒非為一人
===
設也而參之謚益驗蓋使人為善者不直
慶之已也謚美之書褒之萬世之慶也為
不善者不直刑之已也謚非之書貶之萬
世之刑也嗚呼善否一朝慶刑萬世豈可
以私為哉執事發策以書謚之法詢書生
非書生事也然開其略矣六經載道未及
謚法也肇自周公之載籍書以記言未及
書法也肇自孔子之春秋此兩者豈聖人
punctuated:
詳懇到，而詞復高古，殆非凡士。

聖人敎天下之心甚無已也，故有謚法，以定當人之稱名，而榮辱判；有書法，以紀當世之事實，而勸戒昭。聖人何心哉？聖人敎天下以善，而天下率焉，至願也。顧乃有不盡然者，於是不得已而有慶與刑。然慶與刑或有所不及，況行之一時，未能明白㬎著於萬世也。於是不得已而有謚與書。故謚以定稱名，別榮辱，非為一世設也，而考之書益詳；書以紀事實，垂勸戒，非為一人設也，而參之謚益驗。蓋使人為善者，不直慶之已也，謚美之，書褒之，萬世之慶也；為不善者，不直刑之已也，謚非之，書貶之，萬世之刑也。嗚呼！善否一朝，慶刑萬世，豈可以私為哉？執事發策，以書謚之法詢書生，非書生事也，然開其略矣。六經載道，未及謚法也，肇自周公之載籍；書以記言，未及書法也，肇自孔子之春秋。此兩者，豈聖人
translation_en:
…thorough, earnest, and penetrating, while the language is also lofty and antique. Surely he is no ordinary scholar.

The sages’ concern to teach the world never ceases. Thus there are rules for conferring posthumous names, which establish fitting designations for individuals and distinguish honor from disgrace; and there are principles of historical writing, which record the actual events of an age and make encouragement and admonition clear. What is the sages’ intention? Their deepest wish is to teach goodness to the world and have everyone follow it. Yet some fail to do so, and consequently the sages have no choice but to institute rewards and punishments. Rewards and punishments, however, may not reach everyone. Moreover, when applied at a particular time, they cannot remain clearly manifest for ten thousand generations. Thus the sages have no choice but to institute posthumous naming and historical recording.

Posthumous names therefore establish designations and distinguish honor from disgrace; they were not devised for a single age, and examination of the historical record makes their meaning still clearer. Historical writing records actual events and transmits encouragement and admonition; it was not devised for a single individual, and comparison with posthumous names further confirms its judgments. Those who do good are not merely rewarded and then left at that: their posthumous names commend them, and historical writing praises them—rewards for ten thousand generations. Those who do evil are not merely punished and then left at that: their posthumous names condemn them, and historical writing censures them—punishments for ten thousand generations. Alas! Good or evil is done in a single day, but reward and punishment endure for ten thousand generations. How could private partiality be allowed to govern them?

You, honored examiners, have issued a policy question asking a scholar about the principles of historical writing and posthumous naming. These matters lie outside a scholar’s responsibilities, yet I shall set out their broad outlines. The Six Classics convey the Way, but do not yet extend to the rules for posthumous naming; those originated in the records of the Duke of Zhou. The Documents records utterances, but does not yet extend to the principles of historical writing; those originated in Confucius’s Spring and Autumn Annals. As for these two institutions, could it be that the sages…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
好立名號以別白天下後世人哉聖人非
得已也民俗日漓直道浸失善惡無別毀
譽混淆傳世千百沿爲口說即古之仁賢
不得受爲善之利而悖德者且盜名而有
之其害非淺鮮也則所以定右之名垂今
之鑒誅死於前懼生於後者豈容假借於
一字一詞間哉自兩法立而世儒祖之者
有春秋謚法有廣謚有世本有獨斷其後
散之爲十五家之謚人各有見釋古名而
===
附以已意乃其得失互異不盡合古也蓋
有說矣有吳越春秋有楚漢春秋有晉春
秋有唐春秋其後累之爲二十一史之書
代各有史紀時事而裁以古制乃其得失
互異不皆良史也蓋有說矣聖人之爲天
下用法也公而後世或参以私聖人之爲
天下慮患也遠而後世所見者近何也謚
法之立非不疑於議前人之妍蚩也而周
公創之亦曰合人心之同而奉君父之尊
punctuated:
好立名號以別白天下後世人哉？聖人非得已也。民俗日漓，直道浸失，善惡無別，毀譽混淆，傳世千百，沿爲口說，即古之仁賢不得受爲善之利，而悖德者且盜名而有之，其害非淺鮮也。則所以定右之名，垂今之鑒，誅死於前，懼生於後者，豈容假借於一字一詞間哉？自兩法立，而世儒祖之者，有《春秋謚法》，有《廣謚》，有《世本》，有《獨斷》。其後散之爲十五家之謚，人各有見，釋古名而附以已意，乃其得失互異，不盡合古也，蓋有說矣。有《吳越春秋》，有《楚漢春秋》，有《晉春秋》，有《唐春秋》。其後累之爲二十一史之書，代各有史，紀時事而裁以古制，乃其得失互異，不皆良史也，蓋有說矣。

聖人之爲天下用法也公，而後世或参以私；聖人之爲天下慮患也遠，而後世所見者近，何也？謚法之立，非不疑於議前人之妍蚩也，而周公創之，亦曰合人心之同，而奉君父之尊，
translation_en:
…eager to establish names and designations to distinguish people before the world and later generations? The sages had no choice. Popular customs grew daily more debased, and the upright way gradually disappeared. Good and evil went undistinguished; disparagement and praise became confused. Transmitted through hundreds and thousands of generations, these judgments circulated as received sayings. Even the humane and worthy of antiquity could not enjoy the benefits of doing good, while those who violated virtue stole and possessed reputations for it. The harm was by no means slight. Thus, in fixing the reputations of those of old [?], leaving a mirror for the present, condemning those already dead, and instilling fear in those living afterward, how could indulgence be allowed in even a single character or phrase?

After these two methods were established, works by scholars of subsequent ages who took them as their models included Posthumous Designations of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu Shifa), Expanded Posthumous Designations (Guang Shi), Genealogical Origins (Shiben), and Independent Judgments (Duduan). Later, these branched into fifteen schools of writing on posthumous designations. Each author had his own views, explaining ancient designations and adding his own interpretations. Consequently, their merits and faults differed, and they did not conform entirely to antiquity. There is an explanation for this.

There were also the Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue, the Spring and Autumn Annals of Chu and Han, the Spring and Autumn Annals of Jin, and the Spring and Autumn Annals of Tang. Subsequently, historical writings accumulated into the Twenty-One Histories. Each dynasty had its historians, who recorded contemporary events and judged them according to ancient standards. Yet their merits and faults differed, and they were not all good historians. There is an explanation for this too.

The sages applied standards impartially for all under Heaven, but later generations sometimes mixed private interests into them. The sages looked far ahead in anticipating troubles for all under Heaven, but later generations saw only what was near. Why was this? Establishing the rules for posthumous designations was not free from misgivings about judging the merits and failings of predecessors. Yet the Duke of Zhou instituted them, saying only that they accorded with what people’s hearts held in common and upheld the honor due to rulers and fathers…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以天道焉耳善善惡惡定爲世守雖幽厲
不能掩其短况他人乎使此法守之不變
則古道至今存也柰何妄鼓脣吻上下其
議者臧孫辰之縱祀何取於慈惠愛民也
魯人謚之以文管夷吾之崇奢何取於夙
夜儆戒也齊人謚之以敬賈充逆黨也稱
荒幸矣而易之曰武許敬宗佞夫也稱謬
宜矣而易之曰恭若此者何可以一二數
也夫謚以像人譬則畫史之寫照惟肖可
===
也弗肖若父則非若父弗肖若祖則非若
祖豈亦以前人之妍蚩不足議乎謚而若
是無謚可矣愚生之見以爲聖人之慮遠
故公而後之慮近故私也聖人之法在榮
善辱不善乃其心常主於辱不善故曰周
公作謚法而孝子慈孫不能改夫孝子慈
孫所以不能改者必不善之辱也不善者
辱而善益榮矣自秦人欲除謚法曰臣不
得議君子不得議父此其慮在掩護於身
punctuated:
以天道焉耳。善善惡惡，定爲世守，雖幽厲不能掩其短，况他人乎？使此法守之不變，則古道至今存也。柰何妄鼓脣吻，上下其議者？臧孫辰之縱祀，何取於慈惠愛民也？魯人謚之以文。管夷吾之崇奢，何取於夙夜儆戒也？齊人謚之以敬。賈充逆黨也，稱荒幸矣，而易之曰武。許敬宗佞夫也，稱謬宜矣，而易之曰恭。若此者，何可以一二數也？夫謚以像人，譬則畫史之寫照，惟肖可也。弗肖若父，則非若父；弗肖若祖，則非若祖。豈亦以前人之妍蚩不足議乎？謚而若是，無謚可矣。

愚生之見，以爲聖人之慮遠故公，而後之慮近故私也。聖人之法，在榮善、辱不善，乃其心常主於辱不善。故曰：「周公作謚法，而孝子慈孫不能改。」夫孝子慈孫所以不能改者，必不善之辱也。不善者辱，而善益榮矣。自秦人欲除謚法，曰：「臣不得議君，子不得議父。」此其慮在掩護於身
translation_en:
…merely to accord with the Way of Heaven. To commend goodness and condemn evil, establishing this as a rule to be observed for all generations—even Kings You and Li could not conceal their shortcomings under it, much less anyone else. Had this rule been maintained unchanged, the ancient Way would have survived to the present. Why, then, do people recklessly wag their tongues, raising or lowering their assessments? Given Zangsun Chen’s unrestrained sacrifices, how could he qualify as “compassionate, beneficent, and loving the people”? Yet the people of Lu gave him the posthumous name Wen, “Cultured.” Given Guan Yiwu’s devotion to extravagance, how could he qualify as “vigilant and watchful morning and night”? Yet the people of Qi gave him the posthumous name Jing, “Reverent.” Jia Chong belonged to a rebellious faction: he was fortunate to be called Huang, “Dissolute,” yet this was changed to Wu, “Martial.” Xu Jingzong was a sycophant: it was fitting to call him Miu, “Errant,” yet this was changed to Gong, “Respectful.” How could cases like these be counted merely by ones and twos? A posthumous name depicts a person, just as a painter makes a portrait: only a true likeness will do. If it does not resemble your father, it is not your father; if it does not resemble your grandfather, it is not your grandfather. Could one really maintain that the merits and faults of earlier generations are unfit for discussion? If posthumous naming is to be like this, we might as well have no posthumous names.

In this humble student’s view, the sages were impartial because their concerns reached far into the future, whereas later generations were partial because their concerns were shortsighted. The sages’ rule lay in honoring the good and disgracing the wicked, but their abiding purpose centered on disgracing the wicked. Thus it is said: “The Duke of Zhou established the rules for posthumous names, and filial sons and loving grandsons could not alter them.” What filial sons and loving grandsons could not alter must have been the disgrace attached to wickedness. When the wicked are disgraced, the good are honored all the more. When the men of Qin sought to abolish the rules for posthumous names, they said: “A minister must not pass judgment on his ruler; a son must not pass judgment on his father.” Their concern here lay in shielding themselves…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
故孝爲天下慮也乃後有鄭樵者撰謚三
卷謂謚以易名不可加之以惡夫君所云
則舉世皆善人矣不有辱而有榮誰則舍
不善而勉於善乎非聖人意也書法之立
非不疑於行天子之賞罰也而孔子任之
亦曰因周公之後而以南面之權與魯國
焉耳筆筆削削斷自聖心雖游夏不能贊
其詞況他人乎使此法守之不變則古史
不專美也柰何輕操筆端出入其詞者叢
===
宜之在漢摶擊豪右其職也范曄抑以爲
酷吏諸葛亮之在蜀圖列行陣其長也陳
壽誣以非將才李義甫之憸壬而舊唐書
躋與長孫無忌爲伍柳宗元之朋比而新
唐書引與韓愈同傳若此者何可以巨細
舉也夫書以微事譬則律家之斷獄惟當
可也非者是之孰當其非是者非之孰當
其是豈亦以天子之賞罰不見行乎書而
若是無書可矣愚生之見以爲聖人之慮
punctuated:
故孝爲天下慮也。乃後有鄭樵者，撰謚三卷，謂謚以易名，不可加之以惡。夫君所云，則舉世皆善人矣。不有辱而有榮，誰則舍不善而勉於善乎？非聖人意也。
書法之立，非不疑於行天子之賞罰也，而孔子任之，亦曰因周公之後，而以南面之權與魯國焉耳。筆筆削削，斷自聖心，雖游夏不能贊其詞，況他人乎？使此法守之不變，則古史不專美也。柰何輕操筆端，出入其詞者，叢宜之在漢，摶擊豪右，其職也，范曄抑以爲酷吏；諸葛亮之在蜀，圖列行陣，其長也，陳壽誣以非將才；李義甫之憸壬，而舊唐書躋與長孫無忌爲伍；柳宗元之朋比，而新唐書引與韓愈同傳。若此者，何可以巨細舉也？夫書，以微事譬，則律家之斷獄，惟當可也。非者是之，孰當其非？是者非之，孰當其是？豈亦以天子之賞罰不見行乎書，而若是無書可矣。愚生之見，以爲聖人之慮
translation_en:
…Thus filial piety takes thought for all under Heaven [?]. Later there was Zheng Qiao, who compiled three juan on posthumous names. He maintained that a posthumous name replaces a person's personal name and must not impute evil to him. If things were as this gentleman says, everyone in the world would be a good person! If there were honor without disgrace, who would abandon evil and strive toward goodness? This was not the sage's intention.
The establishment of rules for historical writing was certainly open to the suspicion of exercising the Son of Heaven's powers of reward and punishment. Yet Confucius undertook it. His position was simply that, working through the descendants of the Duke of Zhou, he bestowed upon the state of Lu the authority of a south-facing sovereign. Every inclusion and every deletion was decided by the sage's own mind. Even Ziyou and Zixia could not contribute a word, much less anyone else! Had these rules been preserved unchanged, the ancient historians would not alone enjoy distinction. Why, then, do writers wield their brushes so carelessly, arbitrarily including and excluding judgments? When Cong Yi [?] served under the Han, attacking powerful local magnates was his duty; yet Fan Ye disparaged him as a harsh official. When Zhuge Liang served in Shu, planning and deploying battle formations was his strength; yet Chen Shou falsely charged him with lacking a general's talent. Li Yifu was a treacherous flatterer, yet the Old History of the Tang elevated him into the company of Zhangsun Wuji. Liu Zongyuan engaged in partisan collusion, yet the New History of the Tang placed him in the same biographical chapter as Han Yu. How could all such instances, great and small, be enumerated?
Historical writing, to compare it with a lesser matter, is like a legal expert's adjudication of cases: only a fitting judgment is acceptable. If one pronounces the wrong right, who will answer for that wrong? If one pronounces the right wrong, who will answer for that right? Could they likewise suppose that the Son of Heaven's rewards and punishments are not exercised through historical writing? If so, one might as well have no historical writing at all. In my humble view as a student, the sage's concern…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
遠故公而後之慮近故私也聖人之法在
勸善戒不善乃其心常主於戒不善故曰
孔子作書法而亂臣賊子不得肆夫亂臣
賊子所以不得肆者必不善之戒也不善
者戒而善益勸矣自唐主欲自觀史曰知
前日之失爲後來之戒此其慮在飾美於
目前未爲天下慮也乃後有李昉者建言
記注必先以進御然後付之所司夫若所
爲則當世皆善事矣不有戒而有勸誰則
===
去不善而就於善乎非聖人意也愚嘗統
而論之善惡公評在人心古今定論在萬
世前之立論法以教天下而心通乎書周
公所以傳孔子也後之立書法以教天下
而心通乎論孔子所以思周公也是故能
誣于謚不能不取証于書過之小者不以
溢美而失直臧孫辰管夷吾是已罪之大
者不以逃惡而他貸賈充許敬宗是已之
數人者祇足彰謚之者之失耳而於法無
punctuated:
遠，故公；而後之慮近，故私也。聖人之法在勸善戒不善，乃其心常主於戒不善，故曰：「孔子作書法，而亂臣賊子不得肆。」夫亂臣賊子所以不得肆者，必不善之戒也。不善者戒，而善益勸矣。自唐主欲自觀史，曰：「知前日之失，爲後來之戒。」此其慮在飾美於目前，未爲天下慮也。乃後有李昉者建言，記注必先以進御，然後付之所司。夫若所爲，則當世皆善事矣。不有戒而有勸，誰則去不善而就於善乎？非聖人意也。

愚嘗統而論之：善惡公評在人心，古今定論在萬世。前之立論法以教天下，而心通乎書，周公所以傳孔子也；後之立書法以教天下，而心通乎論，孔子所以思周公也。是故能誣于謚，不能不取証于書。過之小者，不以溢美而失直，臧孫辰、管夷吾是已；罪之大者，不以逃惡而他貸，賈充、許敬宗是已。之數人者，祇足彰謚之者之失耳，而於法無
translation_en:
…far-reaching, and therefore impartial; the concerns of later men are immediate, and therefore partial. The sage’s rules aim to encourage goodness and warn against wrongdoing, yet his foremost concern is always to warn against wrongdoing. Thus it is said: “Confucius established rules for historical writing, and rebellious ministers and treacherous sons could no longer act unchecked.” What restrains rebellious ministers and treacherous sons must be the warning against wrongdoing. When wrongdoers are admonished, goodness receives still greater encouragement. When the Tang ruler wished to inspect the historical record himself, he said: “By learning of my earlier mistakes, I can take warning for the future.” His concern lay in embellishing his reputation at that moment; he was not considering the realm. Later, Li Fang proposed that the records of imperial activity must first be submitted for imperial inspection and only afterward handed to the responsible office. If this were done, everything in the current reign would become a good deed! With encouragement but no admonition, who would abandon wrongdoing and turn toward goodness? This was not the sage’s intention.

I have attempted to consider these matters together: impartial judgments of good and evil reside in human hearts; definitive judgments of past and present rest with all succeeding ages. Earlier, the Duke of Zhou established rules for evaluation to instruct the realm, while his intentions accorded with historical writing: this was what he transmitted to Confucius. Later, Confucius established rules for historical writing to instruct the realm, while his intentions accorded with evaluation: this was how he kept the Duke of Zhou in mind. Thus, although posthumous titles may misrepresent a person, one must still seek corroboration in historical writings. For those whose faults were minor, excessive praise does not cause the historical record to lose its fidelity: Zangsun Chen and Guan Yiwu are examples. For those whose crimes were great, their having escaped an adverse posthumous judgment does not earn them indulgence elsewhere: Jia Chong and Xu Jingzong are examples. These men merely expose the errors of those who conferred their posthumous titles; as for the rules, there is no…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
損也能誣于書不能不取証于論信無過
舉貶之不能抑董宣諸葛亮是已苟有疵
行葢之不能蔽李義甫栁宗元是已之數
事者祗足貽書之者之譏耳而於法無損
也然則宜如何由人心之公求聖人之法
因聖人之法師聖人之意欲嚴論法榮辱
並舉可也要主衆衆論而請乞者不得行
欲嚴書法勸戒兩設可也要主覈往牒而
傳訛者不足信何也夫論定於身後以一
===
字槩百年之行亦既難矣而爲之後者生
慕榮位歿慕榮名得之則幸不得不足以
取辱無惑乎請乞之接跡也其衆衆論乎
衆衆論云何辨其人㝠考其行善得善謚
惡得惡謚善惡半者亦如魏謚鄭羲以文
靈唐謚蕭瑀以貞褊瑕瑜不相掩則人不
敢背公而徼私恩矣其庶幾榮辱天下之
法乎夫書成於世遠以一詞括往事之詳
亦既難矣而爲之黨者以無爲有以非爲
punctuated:
損也。能誣于書，不能不取証于論。信無過舉，貶之不能抑，董宣、諸葛亮是已；苟有疵行，葢之不能蔽，李義甫、栁宗元是已。之數事者，祗足貽書之者之譏耳，而於法無損也。
然則宜如何？由人心之公求聖人之法，因聖人之法師聖人之意。欲嚴論法，榮辱並舉可也，要主衆衆論，而請乞者不得行；欲嚴書法，勸戒兩設可也，要主覈往牒，而傳訛者不足信。何也？
夫論定於身後，以一字槩百年之行，亦既難矣。而爲之後者，生慕榮位，歿慕榮名，得之則幸，不得不足以取辱，無惑乎請乞之接跡也。其衆衆論乎？衆衆論云何？辨其人，㝠考其行，善得善謚，惡得惡謚。善惡半者，亦如魏謚鄭羲以文靈，唐謚蕭瑀以貞褊，瑕瑜不相掩，則人不敢背公而徼私恩矣。其庶幾榮辱天下之法乎？
夫書成於世遠，以一詞括往事之詳，亦既難矣。而爲之黨者，以無爲有，以非爲
translation_en:
…no harm to the standard itself. Though written records may misrepresent someone, judgments must still be consulted for corroboration. If a person truly committed no wrongful acts, disparagement cannot diminish him: Dong Xuan and Zhuge Liang are examples. If a person had flaws in his conduct, attempts to cover them cannot conceal them: Li Yifu and Liu Zongyuan are examples. These cases merely expose those who wrote the accounts to criticism; they do no harm to the standard itself.
What, then, should be done? Seek the sages’ standards through the impartiality of the human heart, and follow the sages’ intentions through their standards. To make the standards of judgment rigorous, one may employ both honor and disgrace; the essential thing is to base judgments on collective opinion [?], so that petitions for favors cannot prevail. To make the standards of historical writing rigorous, one may provide both encouragement and admonition; the essential thing is to examine earlier records, so that transmitted errors are not credited. Why is this?
Judgment is settled after death, and to sum up a lifetime’s conduct in a single character is already difficult. Yet a person’s descendants covet an honored position for him in life and an honored name after death. Obtaining it is a stroke of good fortune; failing to obtain it does not suffice to bring disgrace. No wonder petitions for favors follow one after another. Should collective opinion therefore be consulted [?]? What does consulting collective opinion mean [?]? Distinguish the character of the person and investigate his conduct deeply. Let the good receive a good posthumous title and the wicked a bad one. For those whose good and evil are evenly balanced, follow such examples as the Wei bestowal of the posthumous title Wenling upon Zheng Xi, or the Tang bestowal of Zhenbian upon Xiao Yu. If neither flaws nor merits conceal the other, people will not dare turn their backs on impartial judgment to seek private favors. Would this not approach a proper standard for conferring honor and disgrace upon all under Heaven?
Historical accounts are completed long after the age they describe, and to encompass the particulars of past events in a single phrase is already difficult. Yet a person’s partisans represent what did not exist as existing, and what was wrong as…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
是錄之則幸不錄不足以示戒無惑乎傳
訛之盈耳也其覈往牒乎覈往牒云何據
其事深察其心善則書善惡則書惡善惡
半者亦如晉孫盛之書桓溫唐吳兢之書
張說功過略相當則人不敢蔑實而騰虛
譽矣其庶幾勸戒天下之法乎噫愚于是
益信聖人之爲天下慮何其遠而用法何
其公也此書生之言也
第三問
曹樓
同考試官知縣趙　批〔此題場中作者率多浮泛而子獨考核精詳究極指歸是得聲氣本〕
原之妙者
考試官左中允孫　批〔正樂失傳士子言樂者剿述舊聞無所發明此對考索精詳博而有見因〕
元數以求元聲其能審音知樂者耶
考試官左諭德王　批〔是作不膠固舊見有所發〕
明錄之
punctuated:
是，錄之則幸，不錄不足以示戒，無惑乎傳訛之盈耳也。其覈往牒乎？覈往牒云何？據其事，深察其心，善則書善，惡則書惡。善惡半者，亦如晉孫盛之書桓溫、唐吳兢之書張說，功過略相當，則人不敢蔑實而騰虛譽矣。其庶幾勸戒天下之法乎？噫！愚于是益信聖人之爲天下慮何其遠，而用法何其公也。此書生之言也。

第三問
曹樓

同考試官知縣趙，批〔此題場中作者率多浮泛，而子獨考核精詳，究極指歸，是得聲氣本〕原之妙者。

考試官左中允孫，批〔正樂失傳，士子言樂者剿述舊聞，無所發明。此對考索精詳，博而有見，因〕元數以求元聲，其能審音知樂者耶？

考試官左諭德王，批〔是作不膠固舊見，有所發〕明，錄之。
translation_en:
…right. If these accounts are recorded, they count themselves fortunate; if they are not recorded, this does not suffice to serve as a warning. No wonder erroneous reports fill our ears! Should we not scrutinize the records of the past? What does scrutinizing past records entail? Establish the facts and examine the person's intentions deeply: where there is good, record the good; where there is evil, record the evil. Where good and evil are evenly mixed, follow such examples as Sun Sheng's account of Huan Wen under the Jin and Wu Jing's account of Zhang Yue under the Tang, giving merits and faults roughly their due weight. Then people will not dare to disregard the facts and trumpet an undeserved reputation. Would this not approach a method for encouraging and admonishing all under Heaven? Ah! From this I am all the more convinced how far ahead the sages considered the needs of all under Heaven, and how impartially they applied their standards. These are the words of a mere scholar.

Third Policy Question
Cao Lou

Associate Examiner Zhao, Magistrate, comments: “Most candidates writing on this question in the examination hall were superficial and vague. You alone have investigated with precision and thoroughness, pursuing the ultimate purport. You have grasped the subtle principles underlying sound and qi.”

Examiner Sun, Left Assistant Mentor, comments: “The transmission of correct music has been lost. Candidates who discuss music merely repeat received accounts, offering no new illumination. This answer investigates precisely and thoroughly, displaying both breadth and insight. By proceeding from fundamental numbers to seek fundamental tones, might its author be one who can discern sounds and understand music?”

Examiner Wang, Left Admonisher, comments: “This composition does not cling rigidly to received views and offers fresh illumination. Include it.”

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
有作樂之本有作樂之具何謂本參之造
化發之性情達之倫理驗之風俗以還隆
古之盛治者是也何謂具長短之辨多少
之差清濁之判高下之節以求太音之希
聲者是也明於其本矣而不審於其具吾
見音韻之難諧也規度之未備也太和雖
存何以成導和之用至順雖協何以收達
順之功哉世之論樂者往往究心於中和
之理致詳於神化之精而於鍾律諸家之
===
說漫置之不辨曰此器數之小也此節目
之微也聽其言非不美矣大矣而實則不
然夫金石不調后夔無以施其智律呂不
具師曠無所寄其聰故雖聖如仲尼賢如
季札使非樂聲之親接於耳何以學之而
忘味聆之而審音邪昔漢有制氏世掌樂
官然但能紀其音律而不能言其義君子
固深惜之自漢以後通經學古之士類能
因文以求其義而音律之製載籍亡傳則
punctuated:
有作樂之本，有作樂之具。何謂本？參之造化，發之性情，達之倫理，驗之風俗，以還隆古之盛治者是也。何謂具？長短之辨，多少之差，清濁之判，高下之節，以求太音之希聲者是也。明於其本矣，而不審於其具，吾見音韻之難諧也，規度之未備也。太和雖存，何以成導和之用？至順雖協，何以收達順之功哉？世之論樂者，往往究心於中和之理，致詳於神化之精，而於鍾律諸家之說，漫置之不辨，曰：「此器數之小也，此節目之微也。」聽其言，非不美矣、大矣，而實則不然。

夫金石不調，后夔無以施其智；律呂不具，師曠無所寄其聰。故雖聖如仲尼，賢如季札，使非樂聲之親接於耳，何以學之而忘味，聆之而審音邪？昔漢有制氏，世掌樂官，然但能紀其音律，而不能言其義，君子固深惜之。自漢以後，通經學古之士，類能因文以求其義，而音律之製，載籍亡傳，則
translation_en:
There are foundations for making music, and there are means for making it. What are its foundations? They consist in bringing music into accord with the processes of creation and transformation, expressing it through human nature and feelings, extending it through ethical relationships, and testing it against prevailing customs, so as to restore the flourishing governance of high antiquity. What are its means? They consist in distinguishing lengths, differentiating quantities, discriminating between clear and turbid tones, and regulating high and low pitches, so as to seek the rarefied sound of the Great Tone. If one understands its foundations but does not carefully examine its means, I foresee difficulty in harmonizing the tones and deficiencies in the standards and measurements. Even if supreme harmony is present, how can music fulfill its function of fostering harmony? Even if perfect accord is achieved, how can music accomplish its work of spreading that accord? Those who discuss music nowadays often devote themselves to the principles of equilibrium and harmony and elaborate upon the subtleties of spiritual transformation. Yet they casually set aside the various schools’ explanations of bells and pitch standards without examining them, saying, “These are petty matters of instruments and numbers, mere minutiae of procedure.” Their words sound fine and lofty enough, but the reality is otherwise.

If bells and sounding stones are out of tune, Hou Kui has no means of applying his wisdom; if the pitch standards are incomplete, Shi Kuang has no means of exercising his keen hearing. Thus, even someone as sage as Zhongni (Confucius) or as worthy as Ji Zha, unless the sounds of music reached his ears directly, could hardly study it until he forgot the taste of food, or listen to it and discern its tones. In the Han dynasty, the Zhi family held the music office hereditarily. Yet they could only record its tones and pitch standards, and could not explain their meaning—a deficiency that gentlemen deeply regretted. Since the Han, scholars versed in the classics and learned in antiquity have generally been able to seek that meaning through the texts; but as the methods of establishing tones and pitch standards have not been transmitted in written records, then …

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
知之者蓋鮮矣是以爲論愈多爲法愈濟
雖以和峴胡瑗司馬光范鎭諸賢亦不能
以相一也況其他乎古稱議禮之家名爲
聚訟彼議樂者何獨不然在宋徐復氏有
言曰聖人寓器以聲不先求其聲而更求
其器其可用乎此言制律當先審音也朱
子曰審音之難不在於聲而在於律不在
於宮而在於黃鍾此言審音當先求諸黃
鍾也世爲黃鍾之說者曰置一而九三之
===
以爲法實如法得長一寸凡得九寸命曰
黃鍾之宮各因而三之上生者益一分下
生者損一分自是朱子因之以爲清濁之
辨曰五聲之序宮最大而獨濁羽最細而
獨清商之大次宮徵之細次羽而角居四
者之中見於通解鍾律者然也是司馬遷
之說也蔡氏因之以爲多少之辨曰黃鍾
長九寸空圍九分積八百一十分天地之
數始於一終於十其一三五七九爲陽□
punctuated: 知之者蓋鮮矣。是以爲論愈多，爲法愈濟，雖以和峴、胡瑗、司馬光、范鎭諸賢，亦不能以相一也，況其他乎？古稱議禮之家，名爲聚訟，彼議樂者何獨不然？在宋，徐復氏有言曰：「聖人寓器以聲，不先求其聲而更求其器，其可用乎？」此言制律當先審音也。朱子曰：「審音之難，不在於聲而在於律，不在於宮而在於黃鍾。」此言審音當先求諸黃鍾也。世爲黃鍾之說者曰：「置一而九三之，以爲法，實如法得長一寸，凡得九寸，命曰黃鍾之宮。各因而三之，上生者益一分，下生者損一分。」自是朱子因之以爲清濁之辨，曰：「五聲之序，宮最大而獨濁，羽最細而獨清，商之大次宮，徵之細次羽，而角居四者之中。」見於《通解》鍾律者然也，是司馬遷之說也。蔡氏因之以爲多少之辨，曰：「黃鍾長九寸，空圍九分，積八百一十分。天地之數始於一，終於十，其一三五七九爲陽□
translation_en:
…those who understand it are probably few. Thus theories grow ever more numerous and methods proliferate. Even such worthies as He Xian, Hu Yuan, Sima Guang, and Fan Zhen could not reach agreement, much less others! In antiquity, those who debated ritual were described as a gathering of disputants. Why should those who debate music be any different? During the Song, Xu Fu said: “The sages endowed instruments with sound. If one does not first investigate their sound, but instead seeks their instruments, can these be put to use?” This means that establishing pitch standards requires first examining musical tones. Master Zhu said: “The difficulty of examining musical tones lies not in sound but in pitch standards; not in the gong note but in Huangzhong.” This means that examining musical tones requires first investigating Huangzhong, the Yellow Bell fundamental pitch.

Those who explain Huangzhong say: “Set down one and multiply it by three nine times to obtain the divisor. For each full divisor contained in the dividend, obtain one cun in length. The total obtained is nine cun; this is called the gong note of Huangzhong. In each case, proceed by dividing it into thirds: to generate upward, add one third; to generate downward, subtract one third.” Master Zhu drew upon this to distinguish clear and turbid tones, saying: “In the ordering of the five notes, gong is the fullest and uniquely turbid; yu is the thinnest and uniquely clear. Shang follows gong in fullness, zhi follows yu in thinness, and jue occupies the middle among these four.” Such is the account in the section on bells and pitch standards in the Comprehensive Explanation. This is Sima Qian’s theory.

Master Cai drew upon it to distinguish greater and lesser quantities, saying: “Huangzhong is nine cun long; its hollow bore has a circumference of nine fen, and its volume is eight hundred and ten fen. The numbers of Heaven and Earth begin with one and end with ten. Of these, one, three, five, seven, and nine are yang [illegible]…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
者陽之成也其二四六八十爲陰十者陰
之成也見於律呂新書者然也是亦司馬
遷之說也按戴記宮爲君商爲臣角爲民
徵爲事羽爲物而貴賤因以判焉信如朱
子之言也則是濁者貴而清者賤乎按易
傳一生二二生四四生八八生六十四以
至於萬所謂太極也信如蔡氏之言也則
是多者貴而少者賤乎愚生於此蓋不能
無疑矣且以黃鍾九寸上下相生互爲損
===
益者筭之其增減之數少自二分多至於
四寸三分差池不齊夫律曆一道也曆家
二十四氣每氣筭之不差毫釐若一氣短
二分奇又一氣短三分四分奇又一氣短
五分六分奇又一氣短四寸三分奇則月
之大者過於三十月之小者不及二十九
日不惟無以成歲而律管候氣亦不可用
矣況陽氣自冬至以漸而升而律反減焉
氣有餘而管不足陽氣自夏至以漸□□
punctuated: 者，陽之成也。其二四六八十爲陰，十者，陰之成也。見於《律呂新書》者然也，是亦司馬遷之說也。按《戴記》，宮爲君，商爲臣，角爲民，徵爲事，羽爲物，而貴賤因以判焉。信如朱子之言也，則是濁者貴而清者賤乎？按《易傳》，一生二，二生四，四生八，八生六十四，以至於萬，所謂太極也。信如蔡氏之言也，則是多者貴而少者賤乎？愚生於此，蓋不能無疑矣。且以黃鍾九寸上下相生、互爲損益者筭之，其增減之數，少自二分，多至於四寸三分，差池不齊。夫律曆一道也。曆家二十四氣，每氣筭之，不差毫釐。若一氣短二分奇，又一氣短三分四分奇，又一氣短五分六分奇，又一氣短四寸三分奇，則月之大者過於三十，月之小者不及二十九日，不惟無以成歲，而律管候氣亦不可用矣。況陽氣自冬至以漸而升，而律反減焉，氣有餘而管不足；陽氣自夏至以漸□□
translation_en:
…is the culmination of yang. Two, four, six, eight, and ten are yin; ten is the culmination of yin. Such is the account found in the New Book on Pitch Standards (Lülü xinshu), and this too is Sima Qian’s explanation. According to Dai’s Record of Rites, the gong note represents the ruler, shang the minister, jue the people, zhi affairs, and yu things; distinctions of high and low status are thereby established. If Master Zhu’s words are indeed correct, does this mean that low-pitched sounds are noble and high-pitched sounds base? According to the Commentary on the Changes, one generates two, two generate four, four generate eight, and eight generate sixty-four, extending to ten thousand: this is what is called the Supreme Ultimate. If Master Cai’s words are indeed correct, does this mean that greater numbers are noble and smaller numbers base? On this point, I, an unworthy student, cannot but have doubts.

Moreover, if we calculate from the nine-cun Huangzhong pitch pipe, generating pitches upward and downward through alternating subtraction and addition, the amounts added or subtracted range from as little as two fen to as much as four cun and three fen, varying unevenly. Pitch standards and calendrical calculation follow a single principle. Calendar specialists calculate each of the twenty-four solar terms without the slightest discrepancy. If one term were shorter by two fen and a fraction, another shorter by three or four fen and a fraction, another shorter by five or six fen and a fraction, and another shorter by four cun and three fen and a fraction, then long months would exceed thirty days, while short months would fall short of twenty-nine days. Not only would there be no way to constitute a year, but the pitch pipes would also be unusable for detecting the seasonal qi. Furthermore, from the winter solstice, yang qi gradually rises, yet the pitch pipes instead decrease in length: the qi is in excess, while the pipes are insufficient. From the summer solstice, yang qi gradually [two illegible characters]…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而律反增則氣不足而管有餘擬之數而
不齊求其說而不得於是有半律子聲之
議出焉委曲以相符變遷以相就其辨雖
工恐非造化自然之妙也愚嘗求之諸書
於通鑑外紀得劉恕之言焉曰黃帝命伶
倫造律呂自大夏之西阮隃之陰取竹於
嶰溪之谷斷兩節間長三寸九分而吹之
以爲黃鍾之宮於隋志得長孫無忌之言
焉曰傳稱黃帝命伶倫斷竹長三寸九分
===
而吹之以爲黃鍾之宮近世儒家因取是
說以爲元聲而以次推之升陽漸益至於
蕤賓得九寸歸陽漸損至於黃鍾得三寸
九分所謂三分損益者以左右對待言之
隔八相生者以正徵言之雖未必果有得
於天地之元聲然其措意也勤用心也密
矣徒以異於先儒之說也并劉恕長孫無
忌之言舉不之信焉不知君子之論惟其
理而已求之理未必是也雖言之出於聖
punctuated:
而律反增，則氣不足而管有餘。擬之數而不齊，求其說而不得，於是有半律子聲之議出焉。委曲以相符，變遷以相就，其辨雖工，恐非造化自然之妙也。
愚嘗求之諸書，於《通鑑外紀》得劉恕之言焉，曰：「黃帝命伶倫造律呂，自大夏之西、阮隃之陰，取竹於嶰溪之谷，斷兩節間，長三寸九分，而吹之，以爲黃鍾之宮。」於《隋志》得長孫無忌之言焉，曰：「傳稱黃帝命伶倫斷竹，長三寸九分，而吹之，以爲黃鍾之宮。」近世儒家因取是說，以爲元聲，而以次推之：升陽漸益，至於蕤賓得九寸；歸陽漸損，至於黃鍾得三寸九分。所謂三分損益者，以左右對待言之；隔八相生者，以正徵言之。雖未必果有得於天地之元聲，然其措意也勤，用心也密矣。
徒以異於先儒之說也，并劉恕、長孫無忌之言，舉不之信焉。不知君子之論，惟其理而已。求之理未必是也，雖言之出於聖
translation_en:
…yet the pitch-pipe lengths instead increase, so that the qi is insufficient while the pipes are too long. When tested against the numbers, they do not agree; when an explanation is sought, none can be found. Thus arose the theory of half-length pitch pipes and their higher-register tones. Through elaborate adjustments they are made to accord, and through alterations they are made to fit. Ingenious though the argument is, I fear it does not represent the spontaneous subtlety of nature’s workings.
I have sought answers in various books. In the Outer Annals of the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian waiji), I found Liu Shu’s statement: “The Yellow Emperor ordered Ling Lun to make the pitch pipes. West of Daxia, on the shaded side of Ruanyu, he took bamboo from the valley of Xiexi, cut a section between two nodes, three cun and nine fen long, and blew into it to establish the gong tone of Huangzhong.” In the Treatises of the History of the Sui (Sui zhi), I found Changsun Wuji’s statement: “Tradition records that the Yellow Emperor ordered Ling Lun to cut bamboo three cun and nine fen long and blow into it to establish the gong tone of Huangzhong.” Confucian scholars of recent times have accordingly adopted this account, taking this as the primordial tone and deriving the others in sequence. As yang rises, the lengths gradually increase, reaching nine cun at Ruibin; as yang returns, they gradually diminish, reaching three cun and nine fen at Huangzhong. What is called ‘subtracting or adding one-third’ is stated in terms of corresponding positions on the left and right; ‘successive generation at intervals of eight’ is stated in terms of the primary tone and the zhi tone [?]. Although they may not actually have grasped the primordial tone of Heaven and Earth, their deliberation has nevertheless been diligent and their thought meticulous.
Merely because this differs from the explanations of earlier Confucian scholars, people reject it altogether, disbelieving even the statements of Liu Shu and Changsun Wuji. They fail to understand that a gentleman’s judgments depend solely upon principle. If, when examined against principle, a statement is not necessarily correct, even though it comes from a sage…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
賢不敢以苟同也求之理未必非也雖古
之不出於聖賢不敢以爲異也今姑就劉
恕長孫無忌所謂三寸九分者筭之由黄
鍾至大呂增六分由大呂至大簇由大簇
至夾鍾由夾鍾至姑洗由姑洗至仲呂由
仲呂至蕤賔竝增九分由蕤賔至林鍾減
六分由林鍾至夷則由夷則至南呂由南
呂至無射由無射至應鍾由應鍾復至黄
鍾竝減九分蓋大呂當五陰之盛一陽始
===
生則陽雖進而尚弱林鍾當五陽之盛一
陰始生則陽雖退而尚強固宜其增減僅
得三分之二也驗之清濁焉斯黄鍾極清
者也大簇以下以漸而濁至蕤賔而極大
呂次清者也夾鍾以下以漸而濁至林鍾
而極極則以漸而清轉爲黄鍾斯不亦清
者貴而濁者賤乎驗之多少焉則宫聲極
清者也黄鍾爲正宫其數極少故爲君臣
數多於君故商爲臣民數多於臣故角爲
punctuated:
賢，不敢以苟同也；求之理未必非也，雖古之不出於聖賢，不敢以爲異也。今姑就劉恕、長孫無忌所謂三寸九分者筭之：由黄鍾至大呂，增六分；由大呂至大簇，由大簇至夾鍾，由夾鍾至姑洗，由姑洗至仲呂，由仲呂至蕤賔，竝增九分；由蕤賔至林鍾，減六分；由林鍾至夷則，由夷則至南呂，由南呂至無射，由無射至應鍾，由應鍾復至黄鍾，竝減九分。蓋大呂當五陰之盛，一陽始生，則陽雖進而尚弱；林鍾當五陽之盛，一陰始生，則陽雖退而尚強。固宜其增減僅得三分之二也。
驗之清濁焉，斯黄鍾極清者也。大簇以下，以漸而濁，至蕤賔而極；大呂次清者也，夾鍾以下，以漸而濁，至林鍾而極。極則以漸而清，轉爲黄鍾，斯不亦清者貴而濁者賤乎？驗之多少焉，則宫聲極清者也。黄鍾爲正宫，其數極少，故爲君；臣數多於君，故商爲臣；民數多於臣，故角爲
translation_en:
…sages and worthies, one dare not agree uncritically. If examination by reason does not show it to be wrong, then even if the ancient statement did not originate with sages and worthies [?], one dare not reject it as a departure from accepted teaching. For now, let us calculate on the basis of the three cun and nine fen spoken of by Liu Shu and Zhangsun Wuji. From Huangzhong to Dalü, add six fen; from Dalü to Dacu, from Dacu to Jiazhong, from Jiazhong to Guxian, from Guxian to Zhonglü, and from Zhonglü to Ruibin, add nine fen at each step. From Ruibin to Linzhong, subtract six fen; from Linzhong to Yize, from Yize to Nanlü, from Nanlü to Wuyi, from Wuyi to Yingzhong, and from Yingzhong back to Huangzhong, subtract nine fen at each step. For Dalü corresponds to the flourishing of five yin lines, when one yang line first emerges: although yang is advancing, it is still weak. Linzhong corresponds to the flourishing of five yang lines, when one yin line first emerges: although yang is retreating, it is still strong. It is therefore fitting that the increase or decrease should amount to only two-thirds of the usual amount.
Consider this in terms of clear and turbid—that is, high and low—tones: Huangzhong is the highest. From Dacu onward, the tones gradually descend, reaching their lowest at Ruibin. Dalü is the next highest; from Jiazhong onward, the tones gradually descend, reaching their lowest at Linzhong. Having reached the lowest point, they gradually rise, returning to Huangzhong. Does this not show that the high is esteemed and the low is held inferior? Consider this in terms of greater and lesser numbers: the gong tone is the highest. Huangzhong serves as the standard gong; its numerical value is the smallest, and thus it represents the ruler. Ministers outnumber the ruler, and thus shang represents ministers. The people outnumber ministers, and thus jue represents …

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
民事多於民故徵爲事物多於事故羽爲
物不亦少者貴而多者賤乎是故通於清
濁多少之辨明於貴賤尊卑之義而黃鍾
之律可得而言矣然則司馬遷黃鍾九寸
之說非乎曰九寸者蓋黃鍾之終盆之極
而爲蕤賓之管也非愚之私言也九寸黃
鍾之變韋昭嘗言之矣非特韋昭言之也
司馬遷亦曰細若氣微若聲然聖人因神
而存之雖妙必效是遷亦未敢自以爲神
===
而必有待於聖也朱子亦曰古聲既不可
考姑存之以見聲之彷彿以俟後之知樂
者是朱子亦未敢自以爲知而必有俟於
後也今試取所謂九寸與所謂三寸九分
者兹試之築室布灰以候其氣截竹爲管
以求其聲而孰爲正也較之龠合以均其
量實之秬黍以絫其度而孰爲準也然後
以之比歌聲以之齊簫聲以之定十六聲
其是其非必當有相形而不可掩者故程
punctuated:
民。事多於民，故徵爲事；物多於事，故羽爲物。不亦少者貴而多者賤乎？是故通於清濁多少之辨，明於貴賤尊卑之義，而黃鍾之律可得而言矣。
然則司馬遷黃鍾九寸之說非乎？曰：九寸者，蓋黃鍾之終盆之極，而爲蕤賓之管也。非愚之私言也，九寸黃鍾之變，韋昭嘗言之矣。非特韋昭言之也，司馬遷亦曰：「細若氣，微若聲，然聖人因神而存之，雖妙必效。」是遷亦未敢自以爲神，而必有待於聖也。朱子亦曰：「古聲既不可考，姑存之，以見聲之彷彿，以俟後之知樂者。」是朱子亦未敢自以爲知，而必有俟於後也。
今試取所謂九寸與所謂三寸九分者，兹試之：築室布灰，以候其氣；截竹爲管，以求其聲，而孰爲正也？較之龠合，以均其量；實之秬黍，以絫其度，而孰爲準也？然後以之比歌聲，以之齊簫聲，以之定十六聲，其是其非，必當有相形而不可掩者。故程
translation_en:
…the people. Affairs are more numerous than the people, so zhi represents affairs; things are more numerous than affairs, so yu represents things. Is it not the case that what is fewer is esteemed and what is more numerous is held low? Thus, once one understands the distinctions between clear and turbid tones and between greater and smaller numbers, and grasps the principles of noble and base, superior and inferior, one can discuss the pitch standard of Huangzhong.
Does this mean, then, that Sima Qian’s statement that the Huangzhong pitch pipe measures nine cun is wrong? I reply: nine cun is apparently the ultimate limit of Huangzhong’s transformation [?], and is the length of the Ruibin pipe. This is not merely my own humble assertion. Wei Zhao already spoke of nine cun as a transformation of Huangzhong. Nor was Wei Zhao alone in saying this. Sima Qian also said: “Subtle as qi, faint as sound, yet the sage preserves it through its numinous workings; although mysterious, it must have observable effects.” Thus Qian, too, did not presume to possess numinous understanding himself, but necessarily awaited a sage. Master Zhu also said: “Since ancient pitches can no longer be verified, let us provisionally preserve these, to show some semblance of their sounds and await those in later ages who understand music.” Thus Master Zhu, too, did not presume that he himself understood, but necessarily awaited those who would come after him.
Now let us take the purported nine-cun pipe and the purported three-cun, nine-fen pipe and put them to the test: build a chamber and lay out ashes to observe their response to qi; cut bamboo into pipes to seek their sounds. Which is correct? Compare them with the yue and ge measures to calibrate their capacities; fill them with black millet to determine their linear measurements by accumulation. Which provides the standard? Then use them to compare with singing voices, to bring the sounds of the xiao panpipes into accord, and to establish the sixteen pitches. Their correctness or incorrectness must become apparent through comparison and cannot be concealed. Thus Master Cheng…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子曰律取黃鍾黃鍾之聲亦不難定世有
知音者舉上下聲考之自得其正真知言
哉雖然所謂作樂之本者是天地之元聲
也作樂之具者是天地之元數也元數者
律呂長短損益之義雖難言也而夫人固
可能也元聲者乃黃鍾律呂之原雖易言
也而非聖人莫之能也記曰作者之謂聖
述者之謂明今世古制弗存明者何述然
而至樂之在天地間固不容以一日息也
===
聖明之世必將有后夔者出焉神解於曠世之
竊意
後以成鳳儀獸舞之化彼區區得牛鐸而
知爲黃鍾之宮得玉磬而識爲黃鍾之缺
如荀勖張文收者蓋不足言已書生之見
管窺蠡測蓄疑於中久矣謹因明問而質
之
第四問
吳達聰
punctuated:
子曰：「律取黃鍾，黃鍾之聲亦不難定。世有知音者，舉上下聲考之，自得其正。」真知言哉！雖然，所謂作樂之本者，是天地之元聲也；作樂之具者，是天地之元數也。元數者，律呂長短損益之義，雖難言也，而夫人固可能也。元聲者，乃黃鍾律呂之原，雖易言也，而非聖人莫之能也。記曰：「作者之謂聖，述者之謂明。」今世古制弗存，明者何述？然而至樂之在天地間，固不容以一日息也。聖明之世，必將有后夔者出焉，神解於曠世之竊意後，以成鳳儀獸舞之化。彼區區得牛鐸而知爲黃鍾之宮，得玉磬而識爲黃鍾之缺，如荀勖、張文收者，蓋不足言已。書生之見，管窺蠡測，蓄疑於中久矣。謹因明問而質之。

第四問

吳達聰
translation_en:
…Master Cheng said: “The pitch standards take Huangzhong as their basis, and the pitch of Huangzhong is itself not difficult to establish. If someone versed in music examines the higher and lower notes, the correct pitch will naturally be found.” These are truly discerning words! Nevertheless, what is called the foundation of creating music is the primordial sound of Heaven and Earth; what is called the means of creating music is the primordial numerical order of Heaven and Earth. This numerical order comprises the principles governing the lengths of the pitch pipes and their proportional diminution and augmentation. Although difficult to explain, these are certainly within ordinary people’s capabilities. The primordial sound, however, is the source of Huangzhong and all the pitch standards. Although easy to speak of, it can be mastered only by a sage. The Record of Rites says: “One who creates is called a sage; one who transmits is called discerning.” Now that the ancient institutions no longer survive, what can the discerning transmit? Yet the highest music that exists between Heaven and Earth surely cannot be allowed to cease for even a single day. I venture to think that, in an age of sagely enlightenment, someone like Hou Kui will surely emerge, attaining inspired understanding after many generations have elapsed [?], and thereby bringing about the transforming influence that makes phoenixes appear in stately array and beasts dance. Such men as Xun Xu and Zhang Wenshou, who merely obtained a cattle bell and recognized it as the gong note of Huangzhong, or obtained a jade chime and recognized what was lacking in Huangzhong [?], are scarcely worth discussing. My views as a scholar are like observing through a tube or measuring with a ladle; I have long harbored doubts within. Respectfully, I take the opportunity afforded by your illuminating question to submit them for correction.

Fourth Policy Question

Wu Dacong

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭聘　批〔二公以素養之具而操始終不渝之節卓然稱唐宋名臣使千載之〕
〔下讀史者無不興尚友趨思焉是策議論詳悉又能原其仁義忠孝本於性命者他日立〕
〔朝必無愧於二公矣〕
同考試官知州楊　批〔仁義忠孝二公之學術甚正而其志公其節定故能不以顯晦用舍〕
〔二其心此作獨見要領而議論周匝格調俊整可以爲尚論之斷案矣予豈其匹耶〕
考試官左中允孫　批〔宣公文正公才節素定而仁義忠孝寔其大致子能因言知人敷答詳確〕
===
考試官左諭德王　批〔子於古人能論其世而得其生二公之鄉志二公之志者耶試占他日〕
〔其心且詞多感慨可以觀志矣〕
君子之用世也必有經世之具而後其志
定必有礪世之節而後其道隆何謂具學
通帝王之略才周文武之用任之以事而
隨試輙効者是已何謂節器識恢乎遠圖
punctuated:
同考試官教諭聘，批〔二公以素養之具，而操始終不渝之節，卓然稱唐宋名臣，使千載之〕〔下讀史者無不興尚友趨思焉。是策議論詳悉，又能原其仁義忠孝本於性命者，他日立〕〔朝，必無愧於二公矣。〕
同考試官知州楊，批〔仁義忠孝，二公之學術甚正，而其志公，其節定，故能不以顯晦用舍〕〔二其心。此作獨見要領，而議論周匝，格調俊整，可以爲尚論之斷案矣。予豈其匹耶？〕
考試官左中允孫，批〔宣公、文正公才節素定，而仁義忠孝寔其大致。子能因言知人，敷答詳確。〕
考試官左諭德王，批〔子於古人能論其世而得其生二公之鄉志二公之志者耶試占他日〕〔其心，且詞多感慨，可以觀志矣。〕
君子之用世也，必有經世之具而後其志定，必有礪世之節而後其道隆。何謂具？學通帝王之略，才周文武之用，任之以事而隨試輙効者，是已。何謂節？器識恢乎遠圖，
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Pin, Instructor, comments: “With capacities cultivated over many years, these two gentlemen maintained an integrity that never wavered from beginning to end. They stood out as celebrated ministers of the Tang and Song, inspiring all who read their histories a thousand years later to seek their friendship across the ages and aspire to emulate them. This policy essay argues comprehensively and in detail. Moreover, it traces their benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and filial devotion to their roots in human nature and Heaven’s mandate. When its author takes his place at court, he will surely do these two gentlemen credit.”

Associate Examiner Yang, Department Magistrate, comments: “Benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and filial devotion: the learning of these two gentlemen was thoroughly orthodox. Their aspirations served the public good, and their integrity was firmly established. Thus neither prominence nor obscurity, employment nor dismissal could divide their resolve. This composition has a distinctive grasp of the essentials; its argument is comprehensive, and its style elegant and well ordered. It may serve as a definitive judgment in assessing the worthies of the past. How could I be its author’s equal?”

Examiner Sun, Left Mentor, comments: “Duke Xuan and Duke Wenzheng had long been firmly established in talent and integrity, while benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and filial devotion were indeed their guiding principles. You can discern men through their words, and your extended response is detailed and precise.”

Examiner Wang, Left Admonisher, comments: “In considering men of antiquity, you can discuss their times and apprehend their … Were you born in the native region of these two gentlemen, and do you aspire to their aspirations? Let us predict your future … their hearts [?]. Moreover, your language is full of deeply felt reflection, through which your aspirations may be discerned.” [The wording and sequence of this comment appear garbled.]

When a gentleman enters public service, he must possess the capacities to order the world before his purpose can be firm; he must possess the integrity to discipline the world before his Way can flourish. What is meant by capacities? Learning that comprehends the strategies of emperors and kings, talent adequate to both civil and military service, and the ability, when entrusted with affairs, to produce results whenever put to the test: these are what is meant. What is meant by integrity? Breadth of capacity and discernment extending to far-reaching plans …

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
行誼拔乎流俗持之以正而始終不渝
是已其具在我故其始也慨然以天下爲
已任而非以爲名也其節不可奪故其終
也屹然任天下之重而不以苟合也愚生
嘗執此以覽鏡往昔品隲名流三代而下
瑰奇絕特之士負才略而顯功名者何限
乃若全才偉節卓然爲一代純臣者吾於
唐得陸宣公贄其人焉於宋得范文正公
仲淹其人焉夫宣公年十八第進士署渭
===
南簿天下之大計未嘗昔於身也當時所
遣黜陟使者十一輩非有納交之素也而
公汲汲焉以策說之豈以求榮於世哉蓋
使者之職莫先於省風俗聽吏治登雋乂
經財賦保罷瘵簡官事而所以舉其職者
不出乎五術八計三科四賦六德五要之
外其具在我其權在使者况德宗即位之
初遣使巡行天下正世道一新之會也使
吾言朝行而天下夕蒙其惠矣奚必其功
punctuated:
行誼拔乎流俗，持之以正而始終不渝，是已。其具在我，故其始也慨然以天下爲已任，而非以爲名也；其節不可奪，故其終也屹然任天下之重，而不以苟合也。愚生嘗執此以覽鏡往昔，品隲名流。三代而下，瑰奇絕特之士，負才略而顯功名者何限！乃若全才偉節，卓然爲一代純臣者，吾於唐得陸宣公贄其人焉，於宋得范文正公仲淹其人焉。
夫宣公年十八第進士，署渭南簿，天下之大計未嘗昔於身也。當時所遣黜陟使者十一輩，非有納交之素也，而公汲汲焉以策說之，豈以求榮於世哉？蓋使者之職，莫先於省風俗、聽吏治、登雋乂、經財賦、保罷瘵、簡官事，而所以舉其職者，不出乎五術、八計、三科、四賦、六德、五要之外。其具在我，其權在使者，况德宗即位之初，遣使巡行天下，正世道一新之會也。使吾言朝行，而天下夕蒙其惠矣，奚必其功
translation_en:
…conduct that rises above common ways, upheld with rectitude and unwavering from beginning to end: these constitute integrity. Because such capabilities reside in oneself, at the outset one resolutely takes responsibility for all under Heaven, without seeking a name for oneself. Because one's integrity cannot be wrested away, in the end one steadfastly bears the weight of the realm, without compromising merely to win acceptance. This humble student has used these criteria to examine the past and assess its eminent men. Since the Three Dynasties, how innumerable have been the extraordinary men whose talents and strategic abilities brought them conspicuous achievements and renown! Yet for men of comprehensive ability and magnificent integrity, outstanding as wholly faithful ministers of their age, I find in the Tang Lu Zhi, known by his posthumous title as Duke Xuan, and in the Song Fan Zhongyan, known as Duke Wenzheng.
Duke Xuan attained the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) degree at eighteen and was appointed Registrar of Weinan. As for the great affairs of the realm, he never ceased to regard them as his own responsibility [?; the transcription here is unclear]. He had no prior acquaintance with the eleven commissioners then dispatched to assess officials for demotion or promotion, yet he eagerly sought to persuade them with his proposals. Was this to seek worldly glory? The commissioners' foremost duties were to examine local customs, investigate officials' administration, advance men of outstanding talent, manage revenues and taxation, protect the weary and afflicted, and scrutinize official business. The means of fulfilling these duties lay entirely within the five methods, eight plans, three categories, four levies, six virtues, and five essentials. The capabilities lay with him; the authority lay with the commissioners. Moreover, at the beginning of Dezong's reign, when commissioners were dispatched to tour the realm, there was precisely an opportunity to renew the governance of the age. If his words were put into practice in the morning, all under Heaven would receive their benefits by evening. Why must the achievement …

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之自巳出哉文正公以節度推官宅憂觧
任天下之大計亦未嘗責於身也當時宰
執四五輩非有平生之素也而公汲汲焉
以書上之豈以徼名於時哉蓋當世之務
莫急於固邦本厚民力重名器備戎狄杜
姦雄明國聽而所以行之者誠不外乎舉
縣令擇郡守復游散去冗僭慎選舉敦教
育儲將材實邊郡補君過弭民怨保直臣
斥佞人其具在我而其權在宰執况仁宗
===
誠心愛民而一時大臣號稱賢者正世道
向泰之占也苟吾之言行而道亦行矣奚
必於身親爲之哉此其經天下之具素定
於中而其公天下之心不私乎巳故視天
下之事猶一身而視天下之人莫非我君
子於此可以觀二公之大矣記曰事君先
資其言而拜自獻以成其信二公舉進士
登博學宏詞科其言不傳而此二書乃其
筮仕之初志即所謂先資自獻者也厥後
punctuated:
之自巳出哉？文正公以節度推官宅憂觧任，天下之大計亦未嘗責於身也。當時宰執四五輩，非有平生之素也，而公汲汲焉以書上之，豈以徼名於時哉？蓋當世之務，莫急於固邦本、厚民力、重名器、備戎狄、杜姦雄、明國聽。而所以行之者，誠不外乎舉縣令、擇郡守、復游散、去冗僭、慎選舉、敦教育、儲將材、實邊郡、補君過、弭民怨、保直臣、斥佞人。其具在我，而其權在宰執。况仁宗誠心愛民，而一時大臣號稱賢者，正世道向泰之占也。苟吾之言行，而道亦行矣，奚必於身親爲之哉？此其經天下之具，素定於中，而其公天下之心，不私乎巳。故視天下之事猶一身，而視天下之人莫非我。君子於此可以觀二公之大矣。
記曰：「事君先資其言，而拜自獻，以成其信。」二公舉進士，登博學宏詞科，其言不傳，而此二書乃其筮仕之初志，即所謂先資自獻者也。厥後
translation_en:
…must the achievement have originated with himself? Lord Wenzheng, having served as a judicial officer on a military commissioner's staff, had left office to observe mourning for a parent; responsibility for the great plans of the realm had likewise never been laid upon him. He had no longstanding acquaintance with the four or five chief councillors of the time, yet he urgently submitted his letter to them. Could this have been to seek fame in his own day? Among the affairs of that age, nothing was more urgent than securing the foundations of the state, strengthening the people's resources, safeguarding the dignity of official titles and insignia, preparing against the Rong and Di, forestalling treacherous strongmen, and ensuring that the government heard matters clearly. The means of accomplishing these aims lay precisely in recommending district magistrates, selecting prefects, resettling the wandering and unattached [?], eliminating redundant offices and unauthorized privileges, exercising care in selection and recommendation, strengthening education, cultivating men fit to command, replenishing the frontier prefectures, correcting the ruler's errors, allaying popular resentment, protecting upright ministers, and dismissing flatterers. The means lay with me, but the authority lay with the chief councillors. Moreover, Renzong sincerely loved the people, and the great ministers of the time were reputed to be worthy: this was indeed a sign that the world was moving toward peace and prosperity. If my words were put into practice, the Way would also be put into practice. Why must I carry it out personally? Thus, their resources for ordering the realm had long been settled within them, while their concern for the common good of the realm admitted no selfishness. They therefore regarded the affairs of the realm as those of their own bodies, and every person in the realm as part of themselves. Here the gentleman can perceive the greatness of these two lords.
The Record of Rites says: “In serving a ruler, first present one's words; then, on being appointed, offer oneself in service, thereby fulfilling one's pledge.” The two lords attained success in the jinshi examination and the Broad Learning and Grand Literary Talent examination. Their examination writings have not survived, but these two letters express their aspirations at the outset of their official careers. They exemplify precisely what is meant by first presenting one's words and then offering oneself in service. Subsequently …

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
宣公受知德宗召爲翰林學士奉天之幸
艱難危從拨翰裁詔動中機宜卒能彌縫
主闕以感動人心一時定難之功固歸之
文德腹心之助矣非其文武才猷之素具
何以能敏贍若是邪迨其晚躋政府竭節
盡智知無不言不異於侍從獻納之日諸
所建白即吏僕未易數也乃若馭吏恤民
備邊之三疏尤其設施之大者竊計曩所
屬於使臣者公可自見之行矣今試合而
===
觀之其馭吏之三術即前八計聽吏治三
科登雋乂之約也其均節財賦以恤百姓
之六條即前四賦經財實六德保罷瘵之
實也其論沿邊守備之六失即前五要簡
官事之推也幼學壯行後先一揆雖羣姦
沮撓豈肯少貶以隨時哉使德宗盡用其
言則用人行政治邊馭將咸正罔缺貞元
之治當與貞觀比隆矣柰何延齡進而君
志惑公以去就爭之而忠州之命且繼下
punctuated: 宣公受知德宗，召爲翰林學士。奉天之幸，艱難危從，拨翰裁詔，動中機宜，卒能彌縫主闕，以感動人心。一時定難之功，固歸之文德腹心之助矣。非其文武才猷之素具，何以能敏贍若是邪？迨其晚躋政府，竭節盡智，知無不言，不異於侍從獻納之日。諸所建白，即吏僕未易數也。乃若馭吏、恤民、備邊之三疏，尤其設施之大者。竊計曩所屬於使臣者，公可自見之行矣。今試合而觀之，其馭吏之三術，即前八計聽吏治、三科登雋乂之約也；其均節財賦以恤百姓之六條，即前四賦經財實、六德保罷瘵之實也；其論沿邊守備之六失，即前五要簡官事之推也。幼學壯行，後先一揆，雖羣姦沮撓，豈肯少貶以隨時哉？使德宗盡用其言，則用人行政、治邊馭將，咸正罔缺，貞元之治當與貞觀比隆矣。柰何延齡進而君志惑，公以去就爭之，而忠州之命且繼下
translation_en:
…Duke Xuan gained the recognition of Emperor Dezong and was summoned to serve as a Hanlin Academician. During the emperor’s flight to Fengtian, he accompanied him through hardship and danger [?], wielding his brush to draft edicts, each aptly suited to the circumstances. He was ultimately able to remedy his sovereign’s shortcomings and move the people’s hearts. The achievement of quelling the crisis at that time must indeed be credited to the assistance of this trusted counselor and his literary virtue. Had he not long possessed civil and military abilities and strategies, how could he have displayed such ready resourcefulness?

When, later in life, he rose to the chief council, he devoted all his loyalty and wisdom to his duties and withheld nothing that he knew, just as when he had attended the emperor and offered counsel. His proposals were so numerous that even clerks and servants could not readily count them [?]. His three memorials on managing officials, caring for the people, and preparing frontier defenses were especially important among his measures. I venture to think that what he had formerly entrusted to imperial emissaries he could now personally put into practice.

Let us now consider these writings together. His three methods for managing officials summarize the earlier eight criteria for assessing officials’ administration and three categories for promoting outstanding talent. His six provisions for equalizing and regulating revenue and expenditure to care for the common people give concrete expression to the earlier four levies for managing fiscal resources and six beneficent measures for protecting the exhausted and afflicted. His discussion of six failings in frontier defenses extends the earlier five essentials for scrutinizing official affairs. What he learned in youth he practiced in maturity; his earlier and later conduct followed a single standard. Although a host of wicked men obstructed him, would he ever have consented to compromise his principles even slightly to accommodate the times?

Had Dezong fully adopted his advice, appointments and administration, frontier governance and the control of generals would all have been properly ordered, without deficiency. The government of the Zhenyuan era would then have rivaled the flourishing rule of the Zhenguan era. Alas, Yanling advanced, and the sovereign’s judgment became clouded. The duke contested this, staking his continuance in office upon it, yet an order assigning him to Zhongzhou was about to follow…

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
矣豈天未欲平治唐之天下歟文正公以
晏殊薦擢爲集賢校理而伏閤之爭回諭
之忤公身再黜而用於西陲卒能經制內
地鞭笞外夷一時戰守之績固徵之西賊
破膽之謠矣非其文武才猷之素具何以
能踔絕如是耶迨其晚貳台司直言勁氣
百折不回無異於諫垣京兆之日諸所建
白即更僕未易數也乃若召對天章隨上
十事此尤其設施之大者竊計晏所望於
===
宰執者公可身親行之矣今試合而觀之
其曰擇長官精貢舉抑僥倖即所謂固邦
本重名器者也其曰均公田厚農桑減徭
役修武備即所謂厚民力備戎狄者也其
曰明黜陟推恩信重命令即所謂明國聽
杜姦雄者也質言成信始終不渝雖羣邪
震撼豈肯少降以徇人哉使仁宗盡行其
言則紀綱日振國勢日強二虜就服而慶
曆之治不還變爲熙寧紹聖之紛紛矣乔
punctuated:
矣。豈天未欲平治唐之天下歟？

文正公以晏殊薦，擢爲集賢校理，而伏閤之爭、回諭之忤，公身再黜，而用於西陲，卒能經制內地，鞭笞外夷。一時戰守之績，固徵之西賊破膽之謠矣。非其文武才猷之素具，何以能踔絕如是耶？迨其晚貳台司，直言勁氣，百折不回，無異於諫垣京兆之日。諸所建白，即更僕未易數也。乃若召對天章，隨上十事，此尤其設施之大者。竊計晏所望於宰執者，公可身親行之矣。今試合而觀之，其曰擇長官、精貢舉、抑僥倖，即所謂固邦本、重名器者也；其曰均公田、厚農桑、減徭役、修武備，即所謂厚民力、備戎狄者也；其曰明黜陟、推恩信、重命令，即所謂明國聽、杜姦雄者也。質言成信，始終不渝，雖羣邪震撼，豈肯少降以徇人哉？使仁宗盡行其言，則紀綱日振，國勢日強，二虜就服，而慶曆之治不還變爲熙寧、紹聖之紛紛矣。乔
translation_en:
…had already followed. Could it be that Heaven was not yet willing to bring peace and order to the Tang realm?

Lord Wenzheng (Fan Zhongyan), recommended by Yan Shu, was promoted to Proofreader in the Academy of Scholarly Worthies. Yet his remonstrance at the palace gate and his opposition to an imperial reply [?] led to his dismissal twice. Employed on the western frontier, he ultimately brought order to the interior and chastised the foreign peoples beyond. His achievements in warfare and defense at that time are indeed attested by the song about the western rebels’ terror. Without his long-established civil and military abilities and judgment, how could he have distinguished himself so remarkably? When later he became Vice Grand Councilor, his forthright speech and indomitable spirit remained unbent through a hundred setbacks, just as in his days in the remonstrance service and at Jingzhao [?]. His proposals were so numerous that even if the attendants were relieved in shifts, they could scarcely all be enumerated. Among them, his submission of ten measures following his summons to an audience in the Tianzhang Pavilion was especially consequential. I venture to think that what Yan had expected of the chief councilors, Lord Wenzheng could now personally carry out.

Let us consider these measures together. His calls to select local chief administrators, refine recruitment through the examinations, and curb advancement through undeserved favor correspond to what was termed securing the foundations of the state and safeguarding the dignity of official titles and insignia. His calls to equalize public lands, foster agriculture and sericulture, reduce labor services, and improve military preparedness correspond to strengthening the people’s resources and preparing against the Rong and Di. His calls to make demotion and promotion equitable, extend imperial benevolence and trustworthiness, and give weight to commands correspond to ensuring that the state hears clearly and forestalling powerful malefactors. His plain words became trustworthy deeds, unwavering from beginning to end. Though crowds of wicked men assailed him, how could he have consented to yield even slightly to accommodate others? Had Emperor Renzong fully implemented his proposals, discipline and order would have improved daily, the state would have grown stronger daily, and the two hostile powers would have submitted. The good government of the Qingli era would not subsequently have turned into the turmoil of the Xining and Shaosheng eras. [Unclear final character: 乔] …

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
何夏竦謀而飛謗集公且引避丐外而邠
州之命竟下矣豈天未欲平治宋之天下
歟蓋愚於是而益歎君子遇合之難焉夫
士之用世莫大於得君莫重於得公論此
獲上信友聖人所以著爲訓也宣公於德
宗蚤膺簡眷寄以心膂可謂不得於君乎
然格心之言日切而逆耳之聽愈疎於是
謟佞日進而孤立之勢成矣則得君固不
足恃耶文正在宋朝直節正氣率先士類
可謂不得於公論乎然譽者之言日至而
===
忌者之意愈堅於是正士激昂而朋黨之
謗興矣則公論固不足恃耶天直言極諫
藎臣之偉節而多慾者之所讐建政立事
志士之宏猷而循習者之所駭故宣公之
言重於奉天播遷之日而輕於貞元無事
之時豈智於前而愚於後哉猜忌之君可
與共患難而不可與共安樂此范蠡之所
以扁舟五湖也文正之策用於西事經洛
punctuated:
何夏竦謀而飛謗集，公且引避丐外，而邠州之命竟下矣。豈天未欲平治宋之天下歟？蓋愚於是而益歎君子遇合之難焉。夫士之用世，莫大於得君，莫重於得公論。此獲上信友，聖人所以著爲訓也。宣公於德宗蚤膺簡眷，寄以心膂，可謂不得於君乎？然格心之言日切，而逆耳之聽愈疎，於是謟佞日進，而孤立之勢成矣。則得君固不足恃耶？文正在宋朝，直節正氣，率先士類，可謂不得於公論乎？然譽者之言日至，而忌者之意愈堅，於是正士激昂，而朋黨之謗興矣。則公論固不足恃耶？

天直言極諫，藎臣之偉節，而多慾者之所讐；建政立事，志士之宏猷，而循習者之所駭。故宣公之言重於奉天播遷之日，而輕於貞元無事之時，豈智於前而愚於後哉？猜忌之君，可與共患難，而不可與共安樂，此范蠡之所以扁舟五湖也。文正之策用於西事經洛
translation_en:
…Yet [?] Xia Song plotted, and malicious slanders converged upon the lord. He withdrew to avoid the conflict and requested a post outside the capital; an order appointing him to Binzhou ultimately came down. Could it be that Heaven did not yet wish to bring peace and good government to the Song realm? Here I find still greater cause to lament how difficult it is for a gentleman to find a ruler who appreciates him. For a scholar serving the world, nothing is greater than gaining his ruler’s confidence, and nothing weightier than securing the approval of public opinion. This is why the sage set down as instruction the need to win the approval of one’s superiors and the trust of one’s friends. Lord Xuan [Lu Zhi] early received Emperor Dezong’s special favor and was entrusted with service as his closest confidant. Could one say that he had not gained his ruler’s confidence? Yet the more urgently he spoke to rectify the ruler’s heart, the less the ruler would listen to words that offended his ears. Flatterers thus advanced daily, and he was left isolated. Is gaining the ruler’s confidence, then, insufficient to rely upon? Lord Wenzheng [Fan Zhongyan], with his upright integrity and moral vigor, set an example for the community of scholars at the Song court. Could one say that he had not secured the approval of public opinion? Yet as praise for him arrived day after day, the resolve of those who resented him grew firmer. Upright scholars consequently became impassioned, and accusations of factionalism arose. Is public opinion, then, insufficient to rely upon?

Now [?], forthright speech and forceful remonstrance are the noble integrity of a loyal minister, yet they provoke the enmity of those with many desires. Establishing sound government and accomplishing affairs are the grand designs of a resolute scholar, yet they alarm those who cling to customary practices. Thus Lord Xuan’s words carried weight during the flight to Fengtian, but were treated lightly in the uneventful days of the Zhenyuan era. Was he wise before and foolish afterward? One may share adversity with a suspicious and jealous ruler, but cannot share peace and ease with him. This is why Fan Li took a small boat onto the Five Lakes. Lord Wenzheng’s policies were employed in managing affairs on the western frontier [?] …

title: 隆慶元年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之年而沮於政府設施之日豈利於外而
舛於內哉固寵之臣遠之則樂于用人之
長近之則忌於形巳之短此賈誼之所以
厄於長沙也雖然君子能素豫吾才不能
使世之必我用能素立吾節不能必世之
不我撓用之則達吾之才以經世而立業
撓之則伸吾之節以礪世而明道此於世
道有重輕而君子固無所加損也故宣公
嘗曰吾上不負天子下不負所學不恤其
===
他文正亦曰爲之自我當如是其成與否
有不在我者雖聖賢不能必此諸葛武侯
不計成敗利鈍之心也二公之道光明俊
偉此可以識其大矣然愚生又有說焉夫
才者天之所生必有以充拓之而後其挾
持者始大節者人之所立必有以培植之
而後其負荷者始宏此所謂誠與才合者
也故觀二公之大者又當深探其本焉歐
陽永叔謂宣公之言本於仁義呂本中謂
punctuated: 之年，而沮於政府設施之日，豈利於外而舛於內哉？固寵之臣，遠之則樂于用人之長，近之則忌於形巳之短，此賈誼之所以厄於長沙也。雖然，君子能素豫吾才，不能使世之必我用；能素立吾節，不能必世之不我撓。用之，則達吾之才以經世而立業；撓之，則伸吾之節以礪世而明道。此於世道有重輕，而君子固無所加損也。故宣公嘗曰：「吾上不負天子，下不負所學，不恤其他。」文正亦曰：「爲之自我，當如是；其成與否，有不在我者，雖聖賢不能必。」此諸葛武侯不計成敗利鈍之心也。二公之道，光明俊偉，此可以識其大矣。然愚生又有說焉。夫才者，天之所生，必有以充拓之，而後其挾持者始大；節者，人之所立，必有以培植之，而後其負荷者始宏。此所謂誠與才合者也。故觀二公之大者，又當深探其本焉。歐陽永叔謂宣公之言本於仁義，呂本中謂
translation_en:
…in those years, yet were thwarted when he sought to put them into effect in the central government. Could they have been beneficial outside the court but misguided within it? Ministers intent on securing their own favor gladly employ another’s strengths when he is kept at a distance, but when he is close at hand, they resent his exposing their shortcomings. This is why Jia Yi suffered adversity in Changsha. Nevertheless, a gentleman can cultivate his talents beforehand, but cannot ensure that the world will employ him; he can establish his integrity beforehand, but cannot ensure that the world will not obstruct him. If employed, he gives full expression to his talents, ordering the world and accomplishing great works; if obstructed, he manifests his integrity, exhorting the world and illuminating the Way. These circumstances affect the course of the world, but neither add to nor diminish the gentleman himself.
